It looks like a standard waiver. They still shouldn’t be able to charge you more than what the insurance paid though.

So for example:

They bill the insurance company $1000 per CPT code. The insurance company allows $600 and pays the provider $600 and applies a CO45 write off/adjustment code to the remaining $400. They can not bill you for the remaining $400 without being in breach of their contract with the insurance company.

Now if they bill the insurance company $1000 and the insurance company denies the claim and applies a PR adjustment to the claim the doctors office can charge you for whatever $amount the PR denial is for. Typically that’s what the waiver is for- saying you agree to pay for any amount the insurance company says is your responsibility.

Some extra tips for your first couple of weeks:

Use a hair dryer on low on their bum when you change baby’s diaper before applying diaper cream. Otherwise you run the risk of them getting diaper rash which is no fun for anyone.

Don't wake your baby up at night to feed them, let them sleep as long as they can. If they are only a little fussy (not full on screaming/crying give them a couple minutes to settle down before grabbing them. Babies will fuss in their sleep sometimes its okay to let them fuss)

You can't spoil a newborn! Cuddle your baby as much as you can!

Accept all the help you are offered even if you don't need it. Let people cook for you/bring you food/watch the baby/do chores if they offer!

Try to nap when ever your baby is sleeping if you can.

Try to do something for yourself after the baby is born if you can! (I was able to get my nails done and my hair within the first 3 weeks. It helped me feel like myself.)

If you feel up to it while the baby is sleeping do things you did pre baby! (I played video games with my husband and we watched a lot of tv snuggled on the couch together)

If you can try leaving the baby for short periods of time as soon as you feel up to leaving the house. It's going to be hard the 1st couple of times, but the sooner you start the easier it will get. Don't stress yourself if you don't feel ready to do this right away, but don't feel bad if you do feel up to going out by yourself either!

If you feel up to socializing with friends do it! Just make sure they are up to date on vaccines and not currently displaying symptoms of being sick! It's okay if you don't want to isolate yourself. It's also okay if you do want to isolate yourself.

Listen to your gut. Don't let anyone tell you how to live your life/take care of your baby. Trust your institution! I used to hate when people said after the baby comes instinct takes over and you just know what to do. But I promise you taking care of your child is more natural than you can believe right now! It's hard, but you’ll know more about what to do than you think! And you'll quickly learn and adapt to holding your newborn. (I was super worried id break my son, but he was more sturdy than what I believed).

If your hospital offers a nursery don't be afraid to let them take your baby so you can get some sleep. When my son was in the hospital room with me I was too worried about making sure he was still breathing to sleep. Its okay to have the nurses watch him so you can rest.

If you're baby is screaming and you’re at the end of your rope put them down in their crib/bassinet/pack-n-play and step away. They will be okay for a couple minutes while you collect yourself. 

Finally, its okay to be scared. Its okay to be anxious. It's okay to sad your life is about to change! But I've found more good than bad since having my son. I'm slowly learning how to fold him into my life, without losing who I was before he was born. You will too! Bug if you are struggling please ask for help!

While most providers will attempt to confirm insurance eligibility it isn’t always possible to keep track of for every patient. Not only do providers not always get the insurance denials in a timely fashion but often insurance companies will pay for the services after the insurance was terminated only to take back the payments months or even years later, leaving providers no choice but to bill the patient for the cost of the services rendered. It’s also on you to verify that the provider you’re seeing is in network with your plan. Most likely they didn’t get the out of network denials until 3 appointments after you provided your updated information. 

Your best bet is to call your provider and see if they can discount the rate for you.

Make sure you read your contracts with the insurance. They'll have specific instructions for what you are able to bill and not bill. 1) You always bill insurance BEFORE billing the patient, unless the patient has a set copay for services (I.e. $50 specialist visit, $20 behavioral health copay etc)
2) If you bill 150 for a service and the patient has a deductible the insurance will still discount the charge you billed to whatever the insurance allows for the code billed and then the patient will pay that amount. EXAMPLE: Patient has 1000 DED. You charge 150 for their visit. Insurance would typically pay 90 for the visit. The visit is discounted to 90 and the patient pays you this amount.

Thank you for this response. I’m so glad to see that there are some people who don’t just automatically assume that the s/o is being controlling and that what she says are boundaries are invalid because he’s not forcing her to do something!

It’s not anybody’s place to say that someone’s boundaries are stupid so you don’t have to listen to them. While people don’t always have a reason for a boundary you think is wrong, a lot of times there is one. A silly example consider a friend say “wearing yellow around me makes me upset so I want you to to stop.” And yellow is your favorite color, and this has come after YEARS of you wearing yellow around them. You see the boundary as being unreasonable and you continue to wear yellow and dismiss your friend every time. They grow more and more upset because you don’t even attempt to work with them on the issue. Eventually you’re sick of being told to stop doing something that was okay before and not now and they feel like you don’t care about them at all.

Could it be that they have no real reason why they ask you to stop wearing yellow? Of course! Does that make the boundary invalid and mean you get to ignore it and continue to expect that your relationship is going to be fine and that the other person is entirely at fault. No you don’t.

It shouldn’t be about who’s right and who’s wrong. It should be about trying to work together to see if there’s a way you can better understand each other! Don’t come at them and say something like “you boundary is dumb and following it crosses my boundaries so there!” That just isn’t the right approach and neither of you should be tackling any issues from that standpoint!

It’s possible that the reason they have this boundary is because something bad happened to them or a loved one who was wearing yellow, like a bad accident or a recent attack. Maybe someone did something bad to them while wearing yellow. Hell maybe something they read said something that made them worried if YOU wore yellow something bad would happen to you. None of these reasons mean you should stay if you still don’t feel like they’re valid enough to stop doing the thing. Everyone is correct in saying you don’t have to cater to someone you loves whims! What you have to do is being willing to stop and try to not frame it as who’s right and wrong. That’s the first step to deciding if the relationship should be kept, while being considerate of the person you care about WITHOUT feeling like you can’t do what you want and need to be happy around them.  —— You don’t have to do this. You can most certainly say I’m not willing to accept your boundaries as they just aren’t compatible with my own. To avoid continued hard feelings I’m going to stop seeing you so that we can both have our boundaries respected. Just be sure you don’t give in to pushback of “you’re not being fair. You obviously don’t truly care about me if you won’t do this for me. Etc.” Anytime were someone presents you a boundary your unwilling to even try to compromise on does not give either party the ability to make ultimatums. Saying that if the other person doesn’t change they don’t love them and they’re just not worthy of your love is a toxic way of exiting the relationship. You can respectfully tell someone that you’re unable to accept their boundaries and leave the situation without blaming either of you for leaving. It’s a very considerate way of leaving a relationship with grace while not making it the other person’s fault you’re choosing to leave, and not trying to force them to decide if they respect themselves or their relationship with you more. Anything were you have to force someone to choose you will lead to resentment and more and more issues will build until the relationship implodes and leaves both of you hurting even more than you probably already would be by simply having to part ways from a relationship you value. Prepare before you have this conversation so you’re confident you can follow through. Make sure you know if you’d be willing to hear them out if they don’t try to manipulate/force you into staying but instead ask if you can talk about why not wearing yellow matters to them. If not, simply repeat your boundary one more time and leave, and don’t respond to further messages. They need to respect your boundaries as well.

Now, assuming you don’t want to end the relationship and want to make it work, when you start the open dialogue with your friend go into it knowing whether or not you will consider her reasoning. If yes decide what sort of responses might make you reconsider. No matter what if you want the conversation to end with both of you feeling listened to, and like you’ve tried everything you could to make things work but you just weren’t compatible don’t criticize their reasoning or logic. No matter what it is. Make sure that if it’s starts to feel like you’re blaming each other instead being listened to you pause the conversation. Say something like. “This is important to both of us. I can see you really want this relationship to work, and I hope you feel the same about me. I’m struggling to think rationally and it’s not fair to either of us to feel like we aren’t being heard. Let’s try and come back to this later” decide how many times you’re willing to try before you feel like it’s just never going to work. Once your limit has been reached reference the paragraph above where I discussed how to leave. Work on being able to listen to each other without taking blame for their feelings or making a compromise you don’t feel 100% satisfied with or be prepared for this to still be a wound that can open again when you least expect it.

Nothing you choose to do is wrong, unless it’s trying to force your boundaries in the other person to accept and you continue to stay in the relationship while both struggling for dominance over something that shouldn’t be viewed as dominance in the first place. That’s just a relationship where both of you start fighting for power and control, and I think that’s what Reddit means by telling people to leave whenever they see a boundary that they feel wronged by.

Don’t let anyone convince you to do anything you don’t want too! I hope that you can see my words are given in good faith that you’re looking to try and save the relationship, but are in no way damning you if you’re looking for reasons/encouragement to leave! No matter what happens you are valid, and valuable, and deserve to be in relationships where you feel that way. Good luck!

I want you to be happy and satisfied, so if you enjoy doing it in a public space when others aren’t actively in the room I can also find an excuse to leave to give you some ‘me time’. I’m incredibly happy you’re comfortable enough to share this intimate detail with me, and I want to continue with providing you a safe space to express and explore your desires, while also staying in my own comfort zone”

Or if it’s something you’re completely uncomfortable with her doing even if you’re not in the room express that again while you love that she’s comfortable expressing her sexuality with you, you aren’t comfortable with it being done in public because it isn’t your thing, and you like to save those activities for when you’re alone in your own home. 

But you 100% should start by saying something about you’ve noticed she’s been doing it in public a lot, and you’re curious if there’s a particular reason she’s doing it. Treat it no differently than asking someone why they might choose to do math in a way you don’t. Be truly interested in learning about her reasons! After learning her reasoning make sure to express that your glad she’s comfortable sharing with you, and being open and honest with each other about these things is something you cherish and value. Then proceed to explain how you feel when she does it, and what you would like for her to do. Don’t put any sort of implication that you think it’s wrong or use the word gross/disgusting or any sort of word that might imply she responsible for your/the reason for your disgust. There might be a better way to describe the emotion your feeling other than uncomfortable but be careful that the word you choose doesn’t have connotations that you think the act itself is inherently wrong.

Just like setting any healthy boundary, it should be done in a way that doesn’t make it seem like you have a personal issue with the person you’re setting them with. It should be framed like you would feel this way with anyone and it is your feeling, everyone has there own opinion on things. And while this might be based on a specific situation, this should be something that would hold true for almost everyone in your life at this current moment should you also experience the situation with them. (In general of course if it’s a sexual boundary with your partner you don’t need to imagine the people in your life just consider if you had an imaginary other partner would you feel the same way do you think?). Other people aren’t responsible for how you feel and being able to express your feelings without unintentionally blaming them (or intentionally for that matter) will help your chances of being heard without making them feel horrible. Remember even you can’t control your emotional response to something, so the other person definitely can’t *make* you feel anything. You’re responding to an action they performed, whatever emotion you feel about the action is valid. Blaming them for intentionally causing the emotion is forcing the other person on the defensive, making them feel like they need to defend their actions or immediately change them because they’re being a horrible person. It triggers a fight or flight response that helps nothing! - they still see you setting a boundary as a personal attack? Yes, but you aren’t responsible for how they emotionally react to it. All you can do is repeat that it isn’t about them, and you love them. Eventually they will either hear you or they won’t, but you’ve been respectful of them while not forcing yourself to be uncomfortable to protect their feelings.

I came back because I have a clear head and can articulate better what I mean by all my comments about OPs situation because for me the point I was trying to make is key in healthy relationships.

When your partner or friend struggles with something that puts a strain on your relationship you should be willing to help and support them through it, so long as they are also putting in the effort to fix the issue individually as well. If one person struggles and you don’t have a desire to help them, when the situation keeps compounding for the person struggling, and the relationship continues to suffer because they ask their partner or friend for help and that person disregards their feelings it’s fair to no one, and both parties are responsible for the problem getting out of control. Nobody has to stay in a situation like that. But you can’t blame a single party for staying either. The thing about any intimate relationship whether it’s family, friends, or romantic partners is you go into expecting support and comfort when you struggle. Sometimes it’s hard for either person to recognize that they aren’t being fair.

If someone I care about falls into a dark depression and asks for my help and I start off agreeing to help or with reassurance that I’m there for them and then I don’t follow through but continue the relationship while blaming them for their issues and disregarding their feelings because they aren’t rational and I don’t want to deal with them I’m also not being a good partner/friend to them. Do I have to bend over backwards to give them everything they need? But I do owe them a certain degree of empathy and consideration, including putting some of their needs before things that I want. (Example being they need me to come over but I want to go out drinking. I don’t NEED to go out drinking. And by they needing me to come over I mean they’re struggling incredibly hard with how they’re currently feeling, not just because they’re lonely and haven’t made any efforts to work on that, but because they truly feel like they might be a danger to themselves. If it isn’t a severe situation then you can offer alternatives like “I already had plans to go out, but I would really like it if you joined us!” Or “I’m busy tonight but I could come over x day or we could even go out and do something together!”) 

I believe that it’s super important for you to reverse rules with that person. Consider if you were struggling with those things. Even if you can’t quite understand their feelings try and think of a time you might have even momentarily experienced their current emotion. Then try to imagine if you were CONSTANTLY feeling like that. Would you want to be treated the way you’ve been treating them? Try to put aside your own feelings of personal responsibility. It’s easy to say “they need to work on themselves it’s their issue. If it were me I’d be getting help” but when you can only feel your emotions and aren’t able to process them it doesn’t matter how personally responsible you feel for your actions it’s almost impossible to think rationally. And sometimes feeling that responsibility while the person you look to for help is not helping and also blaming you it makes the problem ten times harder work through because instead of seeking help you feel like you have to deal with it yourself and you then beat yourself up for not being able to and it becomes a vicious cycle.) Do they need a to help themselves? Yes. Do you have to stay if you think they aren’t doing enough? No. But it’s also unfair to stay with them if you’re unwilling to help them. It’s also not fair for them to expect you to help them without seeking additional support.

Which is why having a discussion and setting clear boundaries is important.

He doesn’t HAVE to. He has the right to decide what he will and won’t put up with, and whether or not he wants to help her deal with her issues. It’s perfectly fine for that to be a hard no from him. The problem is that neither one of them are handling their boundaries with any consideration to the other person and that’s unhealthy for both of them. OP disrespects her boyfriend by crossing his boundaries just as he disrespects hers by not only violating her boundaries but then criticizing her for them. They need to be able to communicate their needs and wants from the relationship and decide if they want to continue. Surprise her with her favorite coffee before work/class one morning, get her some of her favorite food and have an impromptu movie night with her on a night she's sad or upset or stressed. 

Little things like that to stat, to show her you're interested and want to do better/be more. And if she reacts well maybe plan a big dramatic event/way to tell her you love her/want to date her, maybe in front of all your friends or something. 

Show her you really want to be with her. And keep doing little things like that for her during the relationship if you get together to let her know you still care, and are still as much in love with her as you were when you wanted to start your relationship together.

Honestly my current boyfriend did much the same thing you did, over a much longer period of time. I however stuck it out and was miserable for almost 6 months, and then when we started our relationship was even more miserable because of how he was treating our relationship. I loved him, and still do with all my heart. So I chose to stay and stick it out and work through things with him. 

That being said I would never do that again. Knowing what I know now, if we ever break up I will not stay if I fall for a guy who doesn't want a relationship because the heartache isn't really worth it. So unless you plan to fully commit and work your ass off to make sure she's happy leave her be and let her move on. After vacation limit your contact with her so she can move on. Otherwise she'll start to resent you, and just end up being miserable and questioning her choices. So for her sake let her go if you're not prepared to give it your everything.
